extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical literature / Horace (scholars, translators, general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Literary-critical commentary and annotated translation of selected satires of Horace, describing their scenes, themes, techniques, and intertextual relations. Useful for studying composition, style, and interpretation of Roman satirical poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-scene unity / dramatic scene
rubrics_metrics.description: "The poem gives us a single scene, a battle of wit between two litigants"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose a satire as a single coherent dramatic episode when appropriate: focus the action in one scene to heighten immediacy and comedic effect. The commentary treats the single-scene presentation as a defining structural feature of this poem (Satire VII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Central rhetorical device (pun) as thematic pivot
rubrics_metrics.description: "The main point of the story is found in Persius' pun on the name Rex (king), which he cleverly links up with the propraetor and the propraetor's most famous ancestor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a concentrated linguistic/rhetorical device (e.g., a pun or verbal link) that ties character, theme, and the poem's larger political/historical associations together; such a device can carry the poem's central point and produce comic or ironic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farcical and dramatic elements from early Satura
rubrics_metrics.description: "This little poem, similar, perhaps, to the farcical and dramatic scenes of early Satura"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt elements of farce and stage-like dramatization (rapid exchange, caricatured figures, sudden reversals) when aiming for an early-Satura comic tone. The commentary notes similarity to farcical/dramatic scenes as a compositional choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour and skilful dramatic treatment as markers of compositional maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The delightful humour, the skilful dramatic treatment of the theme, and the poet's well-established position in Maecenas's circle... indicate that this is one of the latest Satires"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a satire's relative maturity or period of composition by the presence of refined humour and controlled dramatic technique; polished comic handling suggests later work in the poet's development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextual linkage and allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: References such as "The Satire is closely connected in subject with Epodes 5 and 17. Virgil's eighth Eclogue may also be compared" and other notes comparing scenes to Homer/Virgil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In both composition and criticism, identify and employ intertextual echoes (other poems, epic models, earlier satirists). Allusions to canonical works (Homeric, Virgilian, etc.) can be used for ironic contrast, homage, or parody; critics use such links to situate a satire in literary tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-heroic technique and epic parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages described as "mock-heroic and based upon the famous scene in the eleventh book of the Odyssey" or comparisons to epic characters (Hector, Achilles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mock-epic or heroic diction/tropes to parody trivial subjects and produce comic contrast. Deliberate parallelism to epic scenes (or elevated diction applied to low subject-matter) is an explicit technique noted in the commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid stagecraft, sensory detail, and comic physicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative points emphasized in commentary: the cracking of the wooden statue, witches' rites, sound effects ("the crack when my fig-wood buttock split"), dramatic visual detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ concrete sensory images, physical actions, and stageable incidents (sudden noises, grotesque sights) to generate humour and to break up narrative exposition; such vivid detail is singled out in the notes as the source of the poem's comic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of colloquial inscriptions and local color
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary notes like "Horace puts into verse form the common inscription" (burial-plot formula) and references to local topography (Esquiline, Agger, Caesar's gardens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground satire in recognizable social/local details and colloquial textual artifacts (inscriptions, legal formulas, monuments) to lend authenticity and to satirize contemporary mores; such anchoring details help produce irony and social commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character contrast and social satire (life choices, manners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory notes and translations that contrast 'pater who kept me chaste' and the ostentation of the senator followed by slaves, or Horace's modest life vs. Tillius the senator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create satirical effect by juxtaposing social types (modest/honest vs. ostentatious/ambitious) and by using concrete examples of behavior, dress, and habit to expose folly or praise virtues; characterization through social contrast is a recurring evaluative point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic pacing and comic timing (including deus ex machina rescue)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Satire IX the poem's resolution hinges on the timely arrival of the plaintiff/opponent acting as a 'deus ex machina' who rescues the narrator from an awkward companion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure episodes to allow for well-timed reversals or rescues; control tempo so that interruptions, sudden appearances, or legal/formal exigencies can serve as comic or structural pivots. Critics note such devices as evidence of dramatic skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of scope / focused narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit in multiple comments: the poems often concentrate on a single incident or tightly bounded set of actions (e.g., single scene in Sat. VII; compact witch-scene in Sat. VIII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor compactness and concentrated focus rather than sprawling narration when composing short satirical pieces; tight scope enhances immediacy and comedic effect, as the commentary repeatedly treats these works as tightly framed episodes.
